title: How hard is it to steal a work of art?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how easy it is to steal a work of art, part of a series on how easy it is to steal various things (after nuclear weapons). They recount the 1990 Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum heist in Boston, the 1911 Mona Lisa theft, the 2004 Oslo theft of The Scream, Dutch art-theft statute of limitations laws, the 2000 Swedish National Museum heist, the 2008 Zurich E.G. Buehrle Foundation gunpoint robbery, a 2001 jeep ramming raid, Holocaust-era art restitution, and the Toledo Museum of Art loan truck theft. They then cover why art is stolen, black-market prices (about a tenth of market value), art laundering through dealers and auction houses, and the due diligence doctrine of good-faith buyers. The episode is cut off mid-discussion.

segments.title: Opening banter and Boston heist
segments.summary: Banter about hating art, then Josh raises the twentieth anniversary of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum heist in Boston, where thieves dressed as police, subdued guards, and took paintings including Rembrandts and a Manet.

segments.title: Mona Lisa theft and ease of art theft
segments.summary: Josh describes the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa by a museum worker who hid in the Louvre, and the fact that it sat unnoticed for days. They argue that art theft is low-tech compared with banks or jewelers.
topics: how easy is it to steal art

segments.title: Museum heists with guns and The Scream
segments.summary: The 2004 armed theft of Edvard Munch's The Scream in Oslo is cited as an example of how easily museums can be robbed. Dozens of major paintings have been stolen in the past twenty years, including twenty Van Goghs in Amsterdam.

segments.title: Dutch statute of limitations on stolen art
segments.summary: The hosts explain Dutch law under which, after twenty years (thirty for public collections or registered heritage items), title to stolen art passes to the thief. They describe a Dutch case where a private detective set up thieves who were caught on handling and laundering charges.

segments.title: Swedish and Zurich heists
segments.summary: Details of a 2000 Swedish National Museum robbery involving a machine gun, spikes on roads, and diversionary bombs, and a Zurich gunpoint robbery of the E.G. Foundation Museum in which four paintings were taken, two later dropped near a car.

segments.title: Jeep raid, war-era art, and Yale Machu Picchu
segments.summary: Mention of a 2001 museum raid where a jeep drove through the front door, the looting of art during wars, Holocaust-era art restitution and lawyers pursuing claims, and Yale's long refusal to return Machu Picchu artifacts to Peru.

segments.title: Stealing art from a Sausalito gallery and Guggenheim transport theft
segments.summary: Chuck jokes about wanting to steal Dr. Seuss paintings at a Sausalito gallery. They recall the theft of paintings from a Toledo Museum of Art loan truck parked at a motel in Strasburg, Pennsylvania, en route to the Guggenheim.

segments.title: Why art is stolen and fencing it
segments.summary: Art theft is described as the third-largest illicit trade, worth an estimated six billion dollars a year. Thieves typically get about a tenth of market value by selling to unscrupulous dealers or passing off high-quality replicas, and stolen works are laundered through successive sales and auctions, as with a stolen Norman Rockwell in Steven Spielberg's collection.

segments.title: Due diligence and good-faith buyers
segments.summary: The hosts explain the good-faith purchaser doctrine and the due diligence standard that art buyers and international police expect, including checking the stolen art register and treating a quick, hasty sale as a red flag. The transcript ends mid-sentence.
